Day-to-Day Operations & SOPs

The step-by-step processes you'll use on a regular basis in this role.

Friendly Fence & Roofing Sales Process: Step-by-Step

This guide is meant to give you a clear understanding of the steps Friendly Fence & Roofing believes should be taken to successfully and proudly sell our roofing/siding/windows/gutters services to customers.

Adherence to this process is mandatory and it has proven to render better results than just improvising.

You are encouraged to incorporate your natural charm, personality and customer service skills to this process, but please remember to follow each step and accomplish the task in each before moving to the next when selling roofing, siding and windows to our customers. This will guarantee that our brands are recognized for their outstanding customer oriented, 5 star experience!

Preparation / Arrival / Meet & Greet (0 - 5 mins in)
Task: Scope neighborhood, identify roof/siding trends that will help you in the conversation. Have your devices ready for action. Introduce yourself and the company in a nice, friendly way and quickly explain to the customer that you will be taking pictures. Deliver a folder and sample booklet so they can get immediately involved with the project by looking at colors. Suggested Language: (After introductions) “Mr. homeowner, before I come inside to talk to you, I’m going to take 8 pictures of your property to get real time measurements using sophisticated software called Hover. This will generate a report that will help me build your free estimate today. Then I will come back inside and ask you questions to help me understand the project . Are you ok with that? It will take me just a couple of minutes.” Suggested Language to transition to next step: No transition language suggested as you will be outside and come back in to speak to customer
Warm up / Questionnaire (6 - 30 mins in)
Task: Establish trust with the customer and find key information to be used in the conversation as you make progress to the close. Gain key information for the sale. Warm up (trust) Find common ground (FORM Questions - Family/Occupation/Recreation/Motivation to establish familiarity using the things you see around you in the home and find a way to relate) Suggested language: “Do you have children? How old are they?” “What do you do for work?” “Do you play….?” “I noticed…” “You mentioned your wife. Does she know I am here? When and IF we get to a point when we need her, we can get her on the phone, correct? (looking to agree) Suggested Language to transition to next step: “So let me ask you…” (jump to questions in Questionnaire (b)) Questionnaire (key information) Ask strategic questions to create “tie-downs” that you can use later. Find out “how to sell them” through questions. First ask a basic question and then ask follow-up questions to understand what is important to them, what they are looking for in a company and how they will fund the project. The most important questions to answer in this step are: Who are the players? When does the customer want this project done? Why am I here? How are you funding this project? Introduce funding and options and get the customer pre-approved.. Suggested language: “What has brought me here today?” “Have you done home improvement projects before?” “How did that go?” “What type of company are you looking for to complete this project?” “How long have you been thinking about this project?” “Is there anyone else that you’re getting input from about this project?” “Have you thought about how you are going to fun in d this project?” (take opportunity to bring up funding opportunities and easy application to get approved) “When would you like this project to be completed?” Suggested Language to transition to next step: (only when ALL 4 points of step 2) “Ok, thank you for all that information, it helps me understand a lot. Here is what the rest of the appointment is going to look like for today...”
3.Expectation Statement/Upfront Contract (5 mins duration after step 2)
Task: Gain mutual agreement that the customer is comfortable with expressing to move forward or not and that the customer understands the next steps in the process. Question: We have gone over a lot of information, do you have any questions? Question: Is there anything else you need to think about or ask anyone about this decision? Question: Do you have about 30-40 more minutes? Expectation Statement Do you have about 30-40 more minutes? Do you have to pick up the kids, take a phone call, or a work meeting??? "With your permission, here is what the rest of our appointment will look like today. First, I'm going to complete an investigation of your roof and siding. This includes walking around the property (and getting into your attic space), this will allow me to take pictures and videos. I will share the pictures and videos with you after my inspection, along with my recommendation. If my recommendation is to repair or replace your roof/siding, then I will be able to share multiple options and prices with you at the end of our conversation today. Next, I will make sure you are comfortable with __________, I'll share with you about our company, I'll show you our materials, and we will talk about the installation process. Now, if you are comfortable with everything, then it's my job to make it affordable. If I make it affordable, then I did my job and I'll be able to get your project on our installation schedule. If not, then I came as a stranger, and I left as a friend. Sounds good?" Important: This step is not just about saying “Hey here's what you can expect as we move forward..” Upfront Contract Now, the most important thing is this, I want you to know that I can take “NO” just as graciously as I can take a “YES.” If for some reason we are not a good fit: I don't see that as being the case, but if it is, this is a “Safe Space.” I want you to feel comfortable telling me “No.” Sounds good?
4. Investigation / Discovery (15 mins duration after step 3)
Task: Take pictures (20+ minimum) and video evidence in the attic or exterior to assess and make a diagnosis. Once this is completed: Suggested Language to transition to next step: “Alright, Let’s take a look at what I found.”
Discovery Presentation (10 minutes duration after step 4)
Task: Present evidence to the customer: Go over pictures and videos from the investigation and let pictures do the talking. You want to know what the customer thinks about what they just saw rather than you trying to analyze what you're showing them. And odds are, guys, that they think it's horrific. And they're going to say something like, "Wow, we had no idea it was that bad." Suggested language (after evidence has been presented): “Now what are you feeling?” “I’m afraid a repair is not going to solve this problem, are we in agreement?” “I’m sorry folks, a repair is not in the cards today, is it?” Suggested language to transition to next step: “Now that it’s been established that we’re looking at a replacement, let’s take a look at the company you may want to have do your project/work on your home”
Ingage (5 - 10 minutes duration after step 5)
Task: Follow the slides in Ingage on your ipad in this suggested order Company story Industry Accreditation (Insurance/License/Master Elite) Testimonials Installation (Game Day) Suggested language to transition to next step: “I bet at this point you’re wondering how much this project is going to cost you. Have you heard of the Cost vs Value Report? Present Cost vs Value Report. Talk about the credibility of this source as an equivalent to Kelly Blue Book for cars and not our own statistics (How much, return on investment, what materials) Suggested language to transition to next step: “Ok, I’ve talked a lot about boring stuff, now this is the fun part. What goes into a roof”
Product Presentation (10 minutes after step 6)
Task: Build the roof/Show difference siding styles showing options of material qualities. Give the idea that customers are building their own roof as you go through the process. Make sure you are: Using the roof in a bag Showing materials of different qualities Packages Suggested language to transition to next step: “After seeing these materials, would you settle for anything less for your roof/home (siding)?”
Final Bridge
Task: Get the customer to commit that there are NO objections other than price and affordability. At this point we have reviewed a lot of information with the customer. See if they have any questions. Ask them if there is anything they need to “think about.” Ask them if there is anyone else they need to run this big decision by. Suggested language to start step: “Other than price and affordability, is there any reason you would not move forward with us today?. No. Great, next step is we’re going to build out your options. As I mentioned in the beginning, we will now build your estimate like this: we transfer the measurements from the hover report I took at the beginning into a data form and we will get 3 options for you. I cannot manipulate numbers. Give me a couple of minutes to build these options for you.” *Create an estimate with the customer (should be done in 5 minutes). You are encouraged to ask the customer to participate in helping you build the estimate.
Pricing Presentation
Task: Gain customer’s preference for the package/option and reasoning behind it and Present EACH of the 3 prices. Suggested language BEFORE PRICING IS SHOWN: “Let’s look at each option in more detail” “Which one of these 3 options works best for you?” OR “Out of the 3 packages/options that we just went over (GBB) which one do you feel fits your needs the best?” [Get answer - customer picks one of the three] “What made you pick that package? Why did you choose that package?” [Be sure to compliment the customer, regardless of their answer]. “I knew you would choose that answer, I didn’t want to say anything, but I had a suspicion you were going to choose that” PRESENT PRICES. BE QUIET. “Now you’ve seen the prices. Has your choice changed at all?” “How do you feel about the price for each option?” [If it has, focus on the different options. It’s imperative that the client understands that the WHO is doing the work is more important than the options themselves - Prompt the customer to evaluate each option].. Suggested language: “Would you like to move forward with this option? - [if No] “Is it the monthly investment or the total cash investment that doesn’t quite make sense to you?” Suggested language to transition to the next step: The language here will be the yes or no of the customer, which will take you to the next step.
Primary Close
Task: Attempt to close and start working on acknowledging, reassuring and overcoming the objections using the information that has been mentioned or even agreed during the previous steps. This is the time to “Clock in” as your job as a sales person begins here to overcome any obstacles. Suggested Language:
Call to Manager
Task: Convey the idea that there may be some price relief (if there is certainty of the will to move forward) by taking advantage of schedule gaps given by changes in logistics with materials or other unforeseen events. For more information on how to properly set up this step see the Scheduling opportunity - Do not ask for the call to happen, but rather introduce it as a way for you to give the customer what he needs. Call Manager every single time Use Domino effect / Jenga to explain how it works with crews Suggested language: (see scheduling opportunity document) “Let’s take a crack at it and find out what it is” Important: Full price is the ONLY price for Sales rep. If a discount is given it has to come from the manager. Always follow the Turn Over Chain (T.O.): Your Manager Whoever your Manager/Leader designates as second/third in command If you are a Manager > Rick > M Shelly
Cool Down - Next Steps
Task: Take away the sale: Resale of why the customer made the right decision. Confirmation that they are committed and there is no reason to back out. Not sold? Take away discounted prices and the original estimate is good for 45 days. Suggested language “Congratulations, it will be a pleasure working on your project. But before I put this in, I want to be absolutely sure, that there is no reason that you may want to turn around and cancel it” Y - Great! “Here is what will happen next”

HELPFUL DEFINITIONS AND VOCABULARY

“Tie Down”: secure a commitment from a potential customer during the sales pitch. It involves asking questions or making statements that encourage the customer to agree to the proposal, either by affirming their interest, confirming details, or moving toward the next step in the sales process.

“Cinch the knot”: Revisiting a decision later in the sales presentation that the customer made when asking questions and getting the "Tie Downs." Tie downs and cinching the knot go hand

and hand.

“The triangle”: Strategy that the sales consultant can use to overcome a price objection by providing the customer with 3 variables to choose from and narrowing it down to the most important top two choices. The customer can only pick two of the three variables forcing them into a decision. The three variables are: Great company and warranties, Great products/Top of the line products, and the cheapest price.

SALES PROCESS STEPS SUMMARY

STEPTASK
Preparation / Arrival / Meet & Greet 5 minsGreeting, Hover pictures, First impression
Warm up / Questionnaire 25 minsConnect at a personal level - trust Gain important information, funding
Upfront Contract 10 minsExpectation statement for outcomes and next steps
Investigation / Discovery 20 minEvidence collection for later discussion - attic pictures / exterior and video
Discovery Presentation 15 minsPresentation of evidence - Problem buy in
Ingage 10 minsValue building (company story, differentiators)
Product Presentation 20 minsProduct options to solve problem
Final Bridge 2 minsConfirmation of no objections other than price
Pricing Presentation 15 minsPricing options to address problem
Primary Close 15 minsAsk for the sale - handle objections
Call to Manager 10 minsScheduling opportunity
Cool Down / Next Steps - however long it takesConfirm sale / next steps if no sale

Sales SOP

Winner’s Circle Sales Process Framework An Adapted Proven System for Building Consistent, Predictable Sales Execution in Home Services

Confidential Document For Internal Use Only: Winner’s Circle Members

Prepared For: Home Service Business Owners and Sales Leaders Committed to Scalable, System-Driven Growth

Last Updated: Jan 2026

Purpose of This SOP This Sales Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) provides a complete framework for building, training, and managing a high-performing sales organization. It is designed to help owners:

  • Create consistency across every sales interaction
  • Protect margins and customer experience
  • Build systems that scale beyond individual performance
  • Increase company value through repeatable, documented processes

How to Use This Framework This document is a reference framework used by high performing home service operators inside Winner’s Circle.

It is not a mandate. It is not a script to follow word for word. It is a proven structure to adapt to each market, team, and set of values.

The goal is simple: Consistency beats motivation.

Top operators do not rely on hero reps or short-term hype. They build systems, habits, and discipline that perform through long sales cycles, busy seasons, rejection, and turnover.

Use this framework to:

  • Create consistency across the sales team
  • Shorten decision timelines without pressure
  • Build trust, credibility, and urgency the right way
  • Train reps faster and coach them more effectively
  • Remove emotion from performance management

Owners who win do not reinvent the wheel. They install one that turns every time.

Section 1: Winner’s Circle Sales Philosophy

At the core of this framework is a consultative sales approach.

The sales process should feel like a conversation, not a presentation. Customers do not want to be sold. They want to feel understood, guided, and confident in their decision.

This framework helps teams:

  • Ask better questions
  • Listen more than they talk
  • Educate without overwhelming
  • Create urgency without pressure
  • Close more deals on the first visit

When executed correctly, every step builds trust, rapport, and momentum.

Section 2: Sales Methodology Goals

Goal 1: Help the Customer Find the Right Solution

This requires more than product knowledge. It requires:

  • Strong questioning
  • Active listening
  • Clear explanations in plain language
  • Emotional intelligence and awareness

Great reps adjust their approach based on the customer in front of them.

Goal 2: Build Trust, Credibility, and Urgency

People buy from people they trust. Trust is built through professionalism, clarity, and confidence.

Reps are not trying to be friends. They are acting as trusted advisors.

Goal 3: Shorten the Decision Timeline

Long decision cycles lead to ghosting, stalled deals, and lost revenue.

This framework helps teams close more business during the first appointment while protecting the customer experience.

Goal 4: Practice Execution Relentlessly

The framework only works if it is used every time. Consistency creates confidence. Confidence creates results.

Section 3: The 10 Step Sales Process Framework

This 10 step process is the backbone of consistent sales execution. It removes guesswork, shortens decision timelines, and creates a professional customer experience that builds trust without pressure. This is a framework, not a script. Owners should coach to the steps, not memorize lines.

Step 1: Arrival and First Impression

Establish professionalism and control. Reps arrive prepared, on time, and respectful of the customer’s home. Appearance, posture, tone, and energy matter immediately.

Step 2: Agenda Setting

Create clarity and set expectations. Reps explain what will happen during the appointment, including inspection, discussion, pricing options, and next steps.

Step 3: Discovery and Rapport

Understand the customer’s situation, priorities, and concerns. Reps ask open-ended questions, listen carefully, and restate what they hear.

Step 4: Needs Inspection

Identify real needs and create urgency. Reps conduct a thorough inspection, document findings, and show issues using photos and simple explanations.

Step 5: Call to Action and Price Conditioning

Prepare the customer for investment decisions. Reps discuss typical costs, explain what impacts price, and ask how customers usually pay for projects.

Step 6: Trust and Company Story

Build confidence in who the customer is hiring. Reps explain company standards, experience, reputation, certifications, people, and warranties.

Step 7: Prescription and Solution

Show how the solution solves the customer’s specific problems. Reps explain the recommended solution in simple terms and tie it directly to pain points.

Step 8: Value Reinforcement

Slow down and reinforce everything included. Reps walk through the full scope of work in detail and highlight how the solution protects the customer’s home.

Step 9: Price Presentation and Decision Window

Present pricing confidently and narrow the decision timeline. Reps present pricing options, explain time-based incentives, and ask for the sale professionally.

Step 10: Wrap Up and Warm Down

Leave the customer feeling confident and respected. For sales, confirm next steps. For no sale, identify the real reason and set a clear follow-up. This process works when it is followed every time. Consistency beats motivation. Discipline beats personality. Systems beat heroics.

Step by Step Objective and Actions

Step 1: Arrival and First Impression

Objective: Set the tone for professionalism, trust, and control. Owner Guidance: Reps are judged in seconds. Appearance, posture, tone, and preparation matter.

  • Arrive early and prepared
  • Park respectfully
  • Maintain a clean vehicle and organized tools
  • Present a professional appearance
  • Display calm, confident energy

Step 2: Agenda, Warm Up, and Rapport

Objective: Create clarity and comfort before inspection. Owner Guidance: Reps should explain what will happen today so there are no surprises. Agenda Should Include:

  • Inspection process
  • Company overview
  • Product and solution discussion
  • Pricing options and timeframes
  • Payment and financing conversation

Step 3: Discovery and Rapport

Objective: Understand the homeowner’s situation, priorities, and pain points. Owner Guidance: Great reps talk less and listen more.

  • Ask open-ended questions
  • Identify emotional drivers behind decisions
  • Confirm understanding before moving forward
  • Avoid assumptions or rushing to solutions

Step 4: Inspection

Objective: Identify real needs and create urgency.

Owner Guidance: Reps conduct a thorough inspection, document findings, and show issues using photos and simple explanations.

No selling yet. The customer must see and agree there is a problem.

Step 5: Call to Action and Price Conditioning

Objective: Prepare the customer for investment decisions.

Reps discuss typical costs, explain what impacts price, and ask how customers usually pay for projects. Financing is introduced naturally. This prevents price shock later.

Step 6: Trust and Company Story

Objective: Build confidence in who the customer is hiring.

Key Behaviors: Reps explain company standards, experience, reputation, certifications, people, and warranties. This step reduces risk in the customer’s mind.

Owner Guidance: Selling begins here.

Step 7: Prescription and Solution

Objective: Show how the solution solves the customer’s specific problems.

Reps explain the recommended solution in simple terms, tie it directly to pain points. Use visuals or samples when possible.

Owner Guidance: Agreement is gained that the solution makes sense.

Step 8: Value Reinforcement

Objective: Slow down and reinforce everything included.

Reps walk through the full scope of work in detail Reconnect features to benefits Highlight how the solution protects the customer’s home and investment.

Owner Guidance: Value must be clear before price is presented.

Step 9: Price Presentation and Decision Window

Objective: Present pricing confidently and narrow the decision timeline.

Reps present pricing options, explain time based incentives when applicable, focus on affordability, and ask for the sale professionally.

Owner Guidance: Persistence is calm and confident, not pushy.

Step 10: Wrap Up and Cool Down

Objective: Leave the customer feeling confident and respected. Key Behaviors: For sales, reps confirm next steps and reinforce the decision. For no sale, reps identify the real reason, set a clear follow up, and preserve the relationship.

Owner Guidance: Reps should never rush out.

Section 4: Sales Hiring and Onboarding Framework

The goal of hiring and onboarding is not speed. It is consistency. This framework helps owners build a repeatable system that protects standards, shortens ramp time, and creates accountability from day one.

Owners should hire for:

  • Coachability
  • Comfort with structure
  • Professional communication
  • Willingness to follow a process

Recommended Hiring Flow

1. Attract the Right Candidates 2. Initial Interview 3. Behavioral Assessment 4. Second Interview 5. Offer and Expectations

Onboarding Philosophy Onboarding is performance preparation, not orientation. Reps should know what success looks like, how it’s measured, and how they earn more opportunity.

Training Structure

  • Week One: Foundations
  • Week Two: Process and Product
  • Week Three: Execution

Performance Benchmarks New reps progress through learning, coached execution, then full standards. Veteran reps are measured on close rate, revenue per opportunity, and process adherence.

Hiring and onboarding are leverage points. When structured correctly they create consistency, reduce chaos, and improve profitability.

Section 5: Sales Coaching and Performance Management

Framework The purpose of coaching is not correction. It is development. Consistent coaching transforms average reps into top performers and protects culture through clarity.

Coaching Philosophy

  • Coaching is a daily habit, not a monthly event
  • Feedback must be specific, timely, and actionable
  • Data drives conversations, not emotion
  • Accountability is a form of care

Coaching Cadence

  • Daily: Huddles and focus
  • Weekly: One-on-one sessions
  • Monthly: Performance reviews

Coaching Framework

1. Observe 2. Diagnose 3. Coach 4. Practice 5. Follow Up

Coaching is the highest return activity in sales leadership. Systems create results. Coaching sustains them.

Section 6: Training Expectations

Training sets the tone for everything that follows. It builds discipline, confidence, and consistency before a rep runs appointments alone.

Training Philosophy Training is where standards are installed. Effort, engagement, and coachability matter as much as talent.

Attendance and Preparation Reps must arrive on time, complete homework, and review prior lessons.

Professional Conduct Respectful interaction, focus, and professionalism are required.

Participation and Engagement Training is interactive. Role play is required.

Accountability for Learning Each rep owns their development and progress.

Readiness and Graduation Reps must demonstrate understanding, confidence, and system use before running solo.

Training is where standards are installed or compromised. Clear expectations protect performance.

Section 7: Customer Interactions

Every customer interaction is an opportunity to build trust or lose it. Customers want to feel heard, respected, and confident.

Core Principle Customers decide emotionally, then justify logically. Reps must adapt to the customer, not rely on a script.

Common Customer Mindsets

1. The Project Is Not a Priority 2. Competing Priorities Exist 3. They Care About Outcomes, Not Products 4. They Do Not Want to Admit Knowledge Gaps 5. They See No Difference Between Providers 6. They Are Unsure How to Pay

Communication Standards Calm confidence, clear explanations, and respectful tone.

Listening and Rapport Ask open-ended questions, restate concerns, and take notes visibly.

Professional Boundaries Friendly, not familiar. Professionalism builds trust.

Emotional Intelligence Notice tone, body language, and engagement. Adjust accordingly.

Customer interactions are about guidance, not persuasion. Consistency builds reputation, referrals, and long-term success.

Section 8: Deposit Collection, Financing, and Notice to

Proceed The point of sale is where clarity and confidence matter most. This stage protects cash flow, confirms commitment, and ensures projects move from agreement to execution without delay or confusion.

Deposit Collection at Time of Sale Confirm commitment and formally secure the project. A deposit signals that the customer is serious and allows the company to begin scheduling and ordering materials.

Financing Conversation Make the project accessible and remove payment friction. Introduce financing as a service, not a fallback.

Notice to Proceed Stage Formally authorize the company to begin work. Confirm the customer’s intent, financial approval, and readiness for scheduling.

This stage protects the business and the customer. Confidence here reflects leadership upstream.

Section 9: Post Sale Communication, Systems, and

Accountability What happens after the sale matters as much as the sale itself. This stage ensures a smooth handoff, protects the customer experience, and maintains internal clarity.

Post Sale Customer Communication Reinforce trust, confirm expectations, and set the tone for execution.

Entering the Job in CRM Ensure clean handoff from sales to operations. Accurate job entry protects margins and scheduling.

Commission Structure Align incentives with behavior, not just revenue. Reward closed deals, process adherence, and documentation accuracy.

Assessment and Ongoing Accountability Ensure reps are executing the process consistently. Use assessments to confirm understanding, identify coaching opportunities, and reinforce expectations.

Sales does not end at the signature. Strong teams win because expectations are clear and enforced after the deal is done.

Section 10: Assessment and Accountability Framework

Assessment is how standards are protected over time. It is not about catching mistakes. It is about reinforcing consistency, identifying gaps early, and coaching before problems show up in results.

Assessment Philosophy Assessment should be objective, consistent, observable, and actionable.

What to Assess

1. Process Execution 2. Communication Quality 3. System and Documentation Accuracy 4. Results and Trends

Visual Assessment Framework

PROCESS                      COMMUNICATION            SYSTEMS                         RESULTS

Did performance reflect

Did they follow the steps?   Did they earn trust?     Did they protect the handoff?

consistency?

Coaching Based on Assessment Assessment should always lead to action.

Assessment Cadence Assess early in training, frequently during ramp up, periodically for veterans, and immediately when performance slips.

Assessment is how culture is maintained. Discipline in assessment creates discipline in execution.

Consistency in assessment creates consistency in results. Appendix: Inspection and Discovery Template

Purpose: Create consistency during discovery and inspection while reducing missed steps.

  • Standardize discovery across reps
  • Shorten ramp time for new hires
  • Coach objectively using documented inputs
  • Reduce rework caused by incomplete inspections

This template supports conversation, listening, and documentation. Use it as a training aid, coaching reference, or quality control tool.

Get into a habit of using the Inspection Form. It contains great questions you will want the answers to. It also demonstrates to the customer that you are detailed, thorough and by taking notes shows that you are listening and caring about what they have to say.

The first page contains the customer general contact information and great questions.

  • Age of the home?
  • How long do you plan on staying in your home? This is extremely valuable information. The longer

they are staying the more you can justify high quality.

  • Why did you choose this neighborhood?
  • Have you completed any other projects?

This is More valuable information for two reasons. This eliminates potential competitive projects and gives you the opportunity to dig into their answers. If they say they added a new deck and had their kitchen remodeled don’t just say “ok, that’s great” and move on. You MUST dig in. Say something like “Wow, when did you have those done?”, “Was it different contractors?”, “How did each project go”. If one went great say something like: “I’m so happy to hear that, I hear so many nightmare stories, so glad you had a good experience, sounds like you would recommend them?” If one went bad say something like: “I’m so sorry to hear that, glad it seemed to work out in the end though” (Only if it did work out on the end) and the dig into what went wrong) “So what happened?” - “what did do without a kitchen for 6 months?” How did that experience make you feel?” This is information you will use during the trust step when you talk about how long we have been in business, the number of completed jobs, our customer satisfaction scores, our BBB rating etc.

  • Do you have any future projects planned?

Again, more valuable information. It lets you know what you may be competing against. Keep in mind you aren’t always competing against other home improvement projects. You can be competing against sports cars, boast, RV’s, vacations, weddings, etc.

  • What is most important to you about your home?

Check all that apply so they know you are listening to them.

  • How long have you been seriously considering getting the work completed?

More good information. Let’s you know how long they have been experiencing issues or perceived issues.

  • What made you decide to get this project taken care of now?

Let’s you know what they have been waiting for, maybe for a specific reason. Example: Possibly just finished paying for children’s college so now they have more disposable income, etc. or maybe they are just procrastinating.

  • What has stopped you?

Ties into the previous question and answers. This is the customer saying it directly, why they have waited.

Using the inspection form is a key part of the discovery process. If the customer contacted us or set an appointment they did it for a reason. They did it because they have some sort of concern. This is the time to find their concerns and dig into any pain points. Finding pain points will help you later in the appointment. Pricing and Ethical Urgency Examples

Purpose: Demonstrate how urgency can be created without pressure.

  • Frame decision windows clearly
  • Reduce stalled opportunities
  • Create momentum without manipulation

Pricing strategies vary by market. Urgency should feel professional, not forced. 30-Day Price Sheet Customer Education and Value Reinforcement

Purpose: Help reps explain cost and value clearly and confidently.

  • Support newer reps in value conversations
  • Reduce price resistance
  • Improve customer understanding and confidence

Customers buy outcomes, not features. Coach reps to translate features into benefits and educate without overwhelming.

Example Cost vs. Value Report (Detroit, MI): https://www.jlconline.com/cost-vs- value/2025/east-north-central/detroit-mi/

HomeWyse Tool Example (Step #5) How to use:

Look up the 2025 CVV report for your city, find the overall cost (notice in the scope of work that price is for 30 square), divide the overall cost by 30 to get a price per square. For Homewyse search by Zip Code. You must sell the source first for the customer to believe and accept this 3rd party data. This is CRUCIAL. If you don’t sell the source and the fact that it’s verified 3rd party data, they will just hear a salesperson’s word which they won’t believe. Also include what additional damage can occur through waiting if there is an active leak or major issues. (A cost of doing nothing – this can tie directly into the needs commitment) Price conditions are based on the number of squares they have and the cost per square in CVV and Homewyse. (The goal here is to show them in the end we can provide our best solution for less than the avg price giving them amazing value)

Selling the Source: Homewyse Homewyse.com is a cost estimation and budgeting tool for home improvement and repair projects. It’s designed for:

Homeowners trying to understand typical project costs Contractors and sales reps who want a ballpark estimate or regional benchmark Estimators creating scope-or-work or budget ranges It’s not a contractor bidding platform or marketplace. It’s an informational estimator that gives price ranges (low-high) for materials, labor, and total project cost.

How Homewyse Builds Its Price Ranges: Homewyse combines multiple data sources to calculate its numbers. While it’s not 100% transparent about its formulas, here’s what’s publicly known and industry-validated.

National Cost Databases: It pulls data from RSMeans, Craftsman Book Company, and similar trade- cost databases. These contain average labor rates, material costs, and productivity rates across the U.S. Local Labor Adjustments: Homewyse adjusts prices based on zip code, using regional cost indices (similar to how insurance companies or appraisers adjust for local cost-of-living and wage rates). A roofing project in Michigan will show lower average labor costs than one in California or New York.

Material & Supplier Inputs: It references current retail pricing from common suppliers (Home Depot, Lowe’s, etc.) for standard-grade materials. Material markups and waste factors are included, generally reflecting what a mid-range contractor would charge.

Typical Contractor Overhead & Profit: Homewyse estimates usually include 13% overhead and 10% profit baked in — not luxury margins, but enough for a small-to-mid-size contractor.

Standardized Labor Productivity: Their models assume average crew efficiency (not the fastest, not the slowest) and industry-standard labor hours for each task, drawn from trade cost guides.

How Accurate Homewyse Really Is:

Pros: It’s a good ballpark reference for consumers and estimators to sanity-check bids.

Cons: It’s not precise enough for formal bids, because it doesn’t account for:

Company-specific labor costs Premium materials or installation challenges Regional supply shortages Insurance, warranty, or sales overhead

“A public cost reference tool homeowners may use before a sales appointment. It’s based on national averages and doesn’t reflect company-specific standards, warranty coverage, or local permitting requirements.”

“Homewyse is a great ballpark estimator, but it doesn’t account for your roof pitch, tear-off layers, underlayment type, warranty coverage, or certified labor standards. All of which directly affect quality and long-term value.”

Compensation and Performance Alignment Model

Purpose: Align incentives with execution, accountability, and profitability.

  • Tie commissions to completed steps
  • Reduce shortcuts and fallout
  • Protect margins and operations

Owner Guidance: Commission plans shape behavior. Reward consistency, reinforce documentation, and support long-term growth. Coaching and Call Review Tools

Purpose: Improve sales execution through review and feedback.

  • Review calls or in-home appointments
  • Identify strengths and coaching gaps
  • Reinforce standards without emotion
  • Track improvement over time

The value is not the technology. The value is the coaching. Focus coaching on one improvement at a time. These tools exist to support the framework, not replace leadership. Owners should introduce tools intentionally, coach to them consistently, and remove anything that adds complexity without value.

Use what fits. Adapt what matters. Ignore what distracts.

Standard Operating Procedure

Lead Sheet Management Monthly Open, Booked, and Declined-to-Schedule Lead Tracking

1. Purpose To ensure every incoming lead is tracked consistently, worked promptly, documented clearly, and moved to the correct monthly status tab based on the final outcome.

2. Scope This SOP applies to all CSRs and team members responsible for reviewing, contacting, updating, or auditing leads in the shared lead sheet. Each month is organized into three primary status tabs: Open Leads, Calls Booked, and Calls Declined to Schedule.

3. Lead Sheet Columns Column Required Information Date Submitted The date the lead was received or submitted.

Client Name The client or prospect name exactly as provided.

Phone/Email The available phone number and/or email address.

Notes Lead Summary

Source The lead source or provider, such as Angi, Networx, or another approved source.

Until the client explicitly denies scheduling an appointment through the chat tab via Service Titan, via Phone call, via Helpwise, the client will remain in Open Leads.

5. Daily Lead-Handling Workflow 1. Open the current month’s Open Leads tab at the beginning of the shift and continue monitoring it throughout the day. 2. Review the lead details before contacting the client, including the name, contact information, source, existing notes, and any Sameday or Hatch conversation. 3. Attempt contact using the approved call and follow-up process. 4. Determine the correct status based on the client response and the rules in this SOP. 5. Move the entire lead row to the correct tab. Do not copy the row and leave a duplicate behind. 6. Verify that all fields moved correctly and that the lead appears only once within the monthly tabs.

6. Three-Day Rule for One- or Two-Ring Disconnects

  • A phone number that rings only once or twice and then disconnects must not be moved to Calls Declined

to Schedule after the first occurrence.

  • The lead must be attempted across three separate days before it may be moved for this reason.
  • Each day’s attempt must be documented in the Notes column.
  • After the third documented day, the lead may be moved to Calls Declined to Schedule if the same result

continues and no other usable contact method is available.

  • If the client answers, responds by another method, or AI has an unresolved conversation with the client,

update the status based on the actual outcome instead of automatically declining the lead.

Example Notes:

  • Day 1 — 7/22, 10:15 AM: Called; rang twice and disconnected. No voicemail available.
  • Day 2 — 7/23, 1:40 PM: Called; rang once and disconnected. Second day
  • Day 3 — 7/24, 4:05 PM: Called; same result. Third day attempted. Moved to Calls Declined to Schedule

— unusable phone connection. Lead Sheet Management SOP 7. Documentation Standards

  • Enter notes immediately after each attempt or conversation.
  • Use clear, factual language. Do not enter opinions or unnecessary personal comments.
  • State why a lead was moved to Calls Declined to Schedule.
  • For booked leads, move the entire row from Open Leads to Calls Booked.
  • Review all existing note activity before contacting the client to avoid repeated questions or conflicting

communication.

8.Quality Check Done Quality Check

  • Booked leads have been moved out of Open Leads.
  • Declined leads include a documented reason.
  • One- or two-ring disconnects were not declined before the three-day requirement was completed.
  • No duplicate rows remain across the month’s status tabs.

9. Escalation Do not guess when the correct status is unclear. Leave the lead in Open Leads, document the concern, and request guidance from the CSR lead or manager before moving it.

2|P a g e Introduction Businesses that scale and attract premium buyers do not rely on luck. They rely on systems.

A sellable company produces a steady stream of high quality opportunities from multiple sources and converts them with discipline. Google LSAs, inbound calls, web forms, referrals, repeat customers, and third party aggregators all play a role in building a diversified lead engine.

Relying on one channel creates risk. Owning many channels creates leverage.

Each lead type demands a different strategy, different language, and different timing. Owners who win understand these nuances and build playbooks their teams can execute consistently.

This manual outlines the scripts, processes, and frameworks needed to convert more leads into booked appointments and more appointments into revenue. It is designed to create repeatability, accountability, and visibility inside your organization.

When your conversion process is documented and consistently followed, you reduce dependency on individuals and increase enterprise value.

That is how you Build It to Sell It.

Expectations for Success Elite teams operate with:

  • Relentless work ethic
  • Clear problem solving thinking
  • Unwavering integrity

These standards form the foundation of scalable operations and buyer ready businesses.

5|P a g e Glossary

6|P a g e Commonly Used Terminology Square (SQ) - The entire roof is measured in squares. 1 square is equal to 100 square feet. Example = 1200 Square feet is equal to 12 Square. Ridge - The ridge of the roof is the horizontal line that is at the roof peaks. Hip - The hip starts at the ridge & slopes downwards towards the drip edge. Valley - The valley is where 2 roof slopes end at the same place. Rake (gable) Edge - Rake is where the ridge ends & it has a slope. Drip (eave) Edge - The lowest part of the roof that has no slope. Flashing – Sheet metal or other material installed on top of the joints of a roof system to prevent water damage Step Flashing - Flashing that goes up the slope against the house. Pitch - How steep the roof is. Pitch is added to the square, hip, valley, rake edge & step flashing. Sheathing - Plywood over entire roof Shingles – Can be made of different materials with the main purpose of protecting underlying sheathing from the weather. Traditionally measured in squares. Trim – Installed to protect the seam in the roof along a hip or ridge Rafters – Wood or metal slats inside your home that support the sheathing and shingles. They act like the skeleton for the roof. Used with a membrane and vapor barrier, which is typically a sheet of plastic blocking air and water from permeating through Underlayment – Water-resistant, paper-like material that is laid over plywood sheathing to seal it from damaging elements such as rain and snow. Layover/overlay - Laying 1 layer of shingles over another Re-sheath/plywood - The wood under the shingles on a roof Tear off - Removing all layers of shingles Re-roof - Remove all old material & replace with new material Partial re-roof - Only replacing a section of the roof, not the entire roof Layers - There may be multiple layers of shingles on the roof Roof Slope – The incline of the roof. It is expressed as a ration of vertical rise to horizontal run, and tells you how many inches the roof rises for every twelve inches in depth. Drainage – The feature of a roof that allows it to shed water

Roof Materials Tiles - Concrete tiles Cedar shake- Wood shingles (typically do not have plywood underneath) Wood Roofing – Can be shingles or tiles Metal Roofing - Large metal sheets. Comes in vertical panels or shingles resembling slate, tile and shake. Stone-coated steel – Interlocking panels made of clay or shingles and is resistant to damage caused by heavy rains Standing Seam Metal Roofing – Named so because the aluminum or steel roofing panels meet in raised seams that interlock to keep moisture out. Asphalt composite shingles – Made from fiberglass base topped with asphalt and mineral granules. Traditional shingles. Sometimes people will call them architectural shingles; this is just a style of asphalt shingle. Solar Tiles – Solar collectors integrated into existing shingles Slate – Waterproof and resistant to mold and fungus Rubber Slate – A type of slate that looks natural and can be cut with a knife to fit intricate roofs

7|P a g e Clay and Concrete tiles – Can withstand damage from tornadoes. Good for warm and dry climates Green Roofs – Covered with plants and can improve air quality, reduce runoff and insulate homes to reduce urban heat islands. Built-up roofing – Heavy roofing consisted of layers of asphalt, tar or adhesive topped with an aggregate and is only for flat roofs Rolled roofing – Consists of long rolls of mineral-impregnated and asphalt-impregnated material topped with mineral granules Membrane roofing – Another choice for flat or very low-pitch roofs. Membrane roofs can be: Neoprene, EPDM (ethylene propylene diene monomer), Chlorinated polyethylene and chlorosulfonated polyethylene sheets, and Polymer-modified bitumens

Roof Styles Gable – Refers to the triangle spot that is formed when the two pitched areas of the roof meet Hip – Slightly more difficult to build and usually has 4 sides. Performs better in high wind areas. Dutch – It is like a hip roof with small gables at either end. Mansard – It is a four-sided design with double slopes that has very steep lower slopes, which can be flat or curved. Flat - Completely flat, no pitch, not super common in residentials home, very common for commercial buildings Shed – Similar to a flat roof but has more pitch Butterfly – Very modern design that is aesthetically unique. It provides plenty of light and ventilation but drainage is a problem Gambrel – Also called a barn roof because it has been extensively used on bards Dormer – It is an addition to an existing roof. It is a window and a roof protruding from the existing slope of the roof. M Shaped – It is a double gable roof featuring two sloped sides that meet in the middle with corresponding slopes on each side.

8|P a g e Customer Funnel

In-Person vs. Insta-Quote Estimate We cannot provide pricing over the telephone! We offer in person, free, no obligation estimates. If a customer just wants a price and does not want to meet for an in-person estimate, we can refer them over to our web page for a ballpark figure with the free insta quote.

In Person Re-Roof

  • All decision makers can be present at the time of the estimate
  • Meets all of the qualifying criteria

Insta-Quote Re-Roof

  • General Contractors
  • Insurance Claims
  • Realtors
  • Rentals
  • People Selling or Buying a Home
  • All Decision Makers are Unable to Attend Estimate

9|P a g e General CRM Data Entry Creating A Customer Record in ServiceTitan

  • Navigate to the Calls Tab
  • Search by Name, Street or Phone and click the Search button to avoid record duplication.
  • Enter the Customer Name (Service Location Name), Address (will validate upon typing in), and all available

contact information and notification preferences.

10 | P a g e

  • Select “Who will pay for the job?” and choose the option that fits the scenario.
  • ‘Customer is the same as the Tenant’ means it is the homeowner that lives at the service location.

‘Customer is different from the Tenant’ means the paying customer or “Bill To” does not live at the service location. For example, a landlord is your customer who is repairing the roof on one of their properties they rent to another family.

  • Click “Create Customer.”

11 | P a g e Book a Job in ServiceTitan

  • From the Calls tab, Search for the Customer name, or add a new Customer if needed.
  • Then select the Customer's location where the work will be performed (Home icon).
  • Complete the relevant fields starting with Job Type.

12 | P a g e

  • The Marketing Campaign can be manually input by clicking the dropdown and selecting the appropriate

campaign (i.e. Self Generated Lead).

  • After all relevant fields have been completed, click Book Job.

15 | P a g e One Party Objection Handling Customer: “It will just be me. She/he doesn’t need to be here. Is this one of those things where we both have to be here?” Marketer: No problem! Let me ask you, what makes you say that // That’s a great question, what makes you ask? Customer: She/he doesn’t want any part of it. She/he doesn’t want to be involved.

IF SO PROCEED TO “A”

Customer: We had another company over and they made us both be there, and we don’t want to go through that again!

IF SO PROCEED TO “B”

Customer: We just are very busy and it’s hard to get us both home together.

IF SO PROCEED TO “C”

****Anytime the customer is extremely belligerent, we can resort to “Last Straw” But the best practice is to go through our process here first.****

A. Marketer: I understand, has anyone ever explained to you why we strongly recommend both parties are there? Customer: No Marketer: Alright, well allow me to share this with you: When it comes to roofing today in 2026, there are so many options, colors, styles, not to mention installation methods. What we have found in ____ years of doing business, is that initially it sounds like a roof is pretty basic, but most people don’t sit around and think about roofing every day, (unless you work here ) so often times there are far more questions from both parties then anticipated initially. With that being said, in order to leave you with the most accurate quote, 9 times out of 10 we end up needing both party’s input. I’m sure you can appreciate that! (wait for acknowledgement/response) IF the answer is YES/I UNDERSTAND: Go to scheduling. Marketer: The good news is, we are very flexible and have opened up our schedule to accommodate all of our homeowner’s busy schedules…is it usually better to catch both of you home during the day or more towards the evening? I am actually going to have a representative in your area on ________, we could stop by at ______ or ______, which works best for both of you? IF the answer is NO, proceed to D.

B. Marketer: Wow! Let me be the first to apologize on behalf of our industry as a whole! Tell me, did they overstay their welcome too? Customer: Yes and wouldn’t leave! Marketer: That’s unfortunately not the first time I have heard that. It’s a sad part of what we do, that some companies have some procedures that just don’t put the customer first. With us, we are just a smaller locally-owned mom and pop’s type of business here so we aren’t talking suits and ties and slick talking “salesmen”. We actually have what we refer to as _______. Has anyone ever explained to you why it is that WE suggest having both people present? When the answer is NO, proceed back to A.

18 | P a g e Saving a Canceling Appointment Customer: I would like to cancel our appointment for ________________ . No problem, I can help you with that. Let me pull up your information here. Ok, just to confirm it looks like we have you at _______________. And we were going to come out and get you (and spouse) some free information on _________? What makes you say you need to cancel?

Customer answer #1: That day just won’t work for us. I understand, now it looks like we had you on for the ______pm, is that normally the best time to catch you both? Customer: Yeah just ______ he’s got to work late after all…. Sure, that makes sense and we appreciate you letting us know! It looks like I am going to have a rep back in your area on ________, we could stop by at ______ or _____ which time works best for both of you?

Customer answer #2: Yeah, but we just decided we are going to wait….. I understand. Let me ask you this, is this a project you folks are EVER going to do? <Proceed to funnel objection handling>

Customer answer #3: Yeah that’s us, I don’t know why my husband/wife set this up, we aren’t going to be doing ______ (Project) anytime soon. I understand that, and that’s actually exactly what your __________ said, he/she said you folks were definitely not ready to buy anything at this point. Does that sound about right? Customer: Yeah, we aren’t doing it now. That’s understandable, let me ask you a question, is this a project you are EVER going to do? Customer: Yes but we are a long way away from that. That makes sense, when the time does come, what time frame did you have in mind? Customer: Probably just in the next couple years. You know it’s funny that’s also exactly what __________ said too! What he/she said was just that you guys knew they needed some upgrading, and you might look at doing the project in the future. That’s all. He/She didn’t give us the impression you folks were ready to make a purchase tomorrow, and to be transparent, we couldn’t install them right now, even if you wanted us to! Really what ______ had said, was that it would probably be ok for us to stop by since we were already going to be in the ________area, just to get you folks some information for consideration for the future. But she/he also said we needed to check with you first, so since I have you here on the phone, it sounds like we need to move the time or date around for you. I know you said __________ (day) won’t work, but is the _____ time usually the best time to catch you (both) around the house generally speaking? <back to scheduling>

The reason being is because they are driving company vehicles and we take safety very seriously; they aren’t permitted to answer or look at their phones while driving. 35 | P a g e Call Script to Prevent “One-Legged” Appointments This picks up at the point of the conversation where the time and date of the appointment is about to be set.

Perfect and is there a spouse in the house there with you? Great and their name is? (If not, ask: is there anyone whose opinion you value on this project?) Let’s pause here for a second and note that this phrasing is much superior to: “Is your husband/wife available?” That question is loaded with potential misunderstanding. There are many terrible home contractor online reviews out there where an angry homeowner rants something along these lines: “They insisted that I needed my husband there to help me make a decision! I was so offended.” This happens more often than you might think. Avoid it by asking the question in a smarter way.

Okay, back to the script. If they answer they are not the sole homeowner, they will identify the other owner in some way, probably as “husband,” “wife,” or “partner.” For the rest of the conversation, use whatever label they used when referring to the other decision maker.

Customer: “No, my [husband/wife/partner] and I own it together.” Appointment Setter: “Okay, excellent. We have found [the product/service you sell] consultations are more productive when all the homeowners are present. What times and days would work best for both you and your [husband/wife/partner] to be there together?” Obviously, set the appointment if the prospect shares times and days that will work. But if they question having to have their spouse or partner there, here’s what not to do. Do NOT say, “That’s our policy.” That’s about the least empathetic response possible and gives the customer no idea why it would benefit them. When was the last time someone said to you “that’s our policy” and it left you with a good feeling? Yeah, never. Instead, use the language the prospect used when questioning it:

“I hear what you are saying:[REPEAT BACK THE CUSTOMER’S CONCERN/OBJECTION] Believe me, you are not the first person to question why this is now a mandatory part of our process. Let me explain what happens whenever we meet with one homeowner.” Note how the above script leads with empathy. Continue along these lines… “Our consultant would meet with one homeowner and thoroughly answer all questions, explain our products in detail, and quote a price based on a homeowner’s precise choices on size, style, color, and material. Then that homeowner would pass that information on to the spouse, and they would have a bunch of questions, too—but different ones. They would also often hate something about what their spouse or partner had chosen for a quote. Every time—and I literally mean every time—our consultant would need to go back and go over everything again and often have to re-do the choices. Do you see how that could happen and create headaches for everyone?” The prospect usually says yes. Regardless of what they answer, continue educating them on the benefits. “We also find that once the homeowners are actually together during an appointment, they see it is more valuable for them to be able to ask questions together and discuss options while an expert is there to answer them in front of both of them. Does that sound beneficial to you, too?” If yes, move to set an appointment. If still no, then consider some of the following…

36 | P a g e Continued Objections Here are strategies for addressing two of the most common objections, even after the value has been explained. Customer: “We’re too busy to find a time that would work for both of us.” Strategic response options: Note your flexible scheduling and ask what could maybe work, just to get them thinking of it as a possibility. You can also respond that it always takes even more time for everyone to have follow-up appointments. For busy people, one-stop shopping is the superior choice. The other common objection is to keep insisting they can accurately convey the information. Customer: “I am sure I can pass this along to my [husband/wife/partner]. They trust me on this.” Strategic response: “Of course. It’s not so much a matter of being able to pass along the information. It’s just that we do these consultations all the time. The couples always have different questions and emphasize different concerns. The process is much more efficient when we can answer everything at once, and the couples can hear and discuss the answers in real time with each other.”

If Nothing Works, What’s Your Plan? If the prospect still continues to object, you need to make a decision about whether a one-legged appointment has enough potential value to you as a lead. If you aren’t sure, crunch the numbers and see what your close rate is when compared to appointments with both homeowners. You may not have this data, but if you are doing one-leggers, you should start tracking it to get a grip on it. If you feel that the value of one-legger appointments is too low, then end the script this way: “I am so sorry that we aren’t able to accommodate your request for having only one of the homeowners present for an appointment. As I said, it used to cause headaches for us and, even worse, stressed out homeowners when it added time and miscommunications into the process. We are fortunate to be busy because our customers love us and spread the word. Because of all that, I can’t set an appointment now with only one decision maker present. Can I invite you to call us back at any time if you change your mind about an appointment with both homeowners present?”

Final Step If an appointment does get made for both homeowners, end the script by repeating the appointment date and time and confirming the contact information for both homeowners. Then remind the homeowner of the value of both being there one more time with a final sentence: “We look forward to your consultation, and to meeting you and your [husband/wife/partner] and getting both of you what you need to make an informed decision. Thank you and feel free to reach out at any point to reschedule if something comes up for either of you.” And one last tip… Since you will be collecting contact information for both homeowners, confirm the appointment the day before with the one you did not talk to when setting the appointment. This gives a little extra insurance that both parties will be there. Despite your best efforts, we know sometimes one-legged appointments can still happen; homeowners do not always call to reschedule when someone won’t be there. Still, a solid call script will help keep these to a minimum, and help you close more sales, and with greater efficiency.

37 | P a g e Lead Aggregator Best Practices

SPEED to LEAD is crucial. Response time is one of the most important pieces to the puzzle when it comes to fielding leads of any sort. Remember, when someone fills out a lead form, they are at the height of excitement. At this moment the customer took action and any time that passes after that moment we run the risk of them changing their mind, life happening, or another competitor getting to them first. The goal is to make the first contact in 60 seconds or less.

Lead Aggregators: These companies such as Home Advisor, Remodeling.com, Modernize, Goodzer, 1800- remodeling, etc use a variety of tactics, landing pages, and internet capture forms to solicit customers for home improvements. Lead capture forms usually don’t say the name of the Aggregator the lead will be sent to. So, for instance if John and Mary go online and search for “replacement windows for our home” they may end up on a landing page that says: “Fill this out for a free quote.” “Low-cost roofing program click here.” “Want to connect with reputable pros near you? We will connect you!”

The slower the searches, the more aggressive the lead aggregator must get in order to solicit enough leads. The Lead Aggravator then takes the customer’s information, and (unless you have an exclusive lead program) they sell it to 3-5 different companies. Now remember, the customer doesn’t realize what they filled out or who they wanted to come over, they are pretty much oblivious, so we have to build rapport and trust when we get them on the phone. It also means they won’t remember which site it was, and it likely wouldn’t match the name of the company anyway. For that reason, we don’t say “we got your name from Home advisor.” It creates confusion in the initial few seconds, and on this type of lead source we can’t afford that luxury. They have to feel comfortable that we are going to take their hand and walk them through the process. For this reason, our first line of “I received a message you were online looking for information on a ____ project for your home.” Is the best way to begin. Any other verbiage about replacement, appointments, coming over, could set off resistance if they were simply just looking for options and pricing.

The first response, as soon as the lead comes in via email, text, phone call, is to respond to it in 60 seconds or less. If we wait, our likelihood of getting ahold of them at all dwindles at lightning speed.

Aggregator Cadences: 1. Call in 60 seconds or less! 2. Call back immediately if they don’t answer. 3. Send a text. 4. Call again 5 minutes later. 5. Call again at the 1-hour mark. 6. Call once more at the 5-hour mark. 7. The next day, call once in the morning and once in the evening. 8. Text the next day as well. 9. Continue texting pattern of texting 1x per week for the first 30 days. 10. Continue to call pattern of 2x per day until they buy or die.

38 | P a g e Take a moment to put yourself in the customer’s mindset. You fill out a form online and start getting bombarded with calls. From companies you may not like or have never heard of…. from pushy to pushovers. One right after another. How do we set ourselves apart? How do we overcome a frustrated homeowner if we are the 3rd call, they have answered in the past 10 minutes? All great things to consider. We have scripting available to help set you apart in the first few seconds of the call! Remember the customer many times will respond with what we call a conditioned response: “I don’t need anything.” “I can’t talk- I’m at work.” “I’m driving” “I’m not interested.” “I don’t know what you are talking about.” “I didn’t fill anything out.”

These are said out of habit, they are not actual objections. We need to use our script for Objections in the First 20 seconds to build a bridge and get past these. If we get them into the need uncovering conversation, the lead will often set itself. But we have to make sure we are not letting people off the hook with conditioned responses. We must believe their actions (they filled out the form) over the words (not interested). Their mouth will tell us what they want us to believe, and their actions tell us what they truly believe. If they couldn’t talk, they wouldn’t have answered the phone. Remember, once we use our Objections in the first 20 seconds, it will disarm the prospect, and then we have a chance.

Industry standard raw to set percentage should be 20-30%, so keep realistic expectations.

39 | P a g e Rehash Sign-Up Appointment Procedure

What Qualifies a rehash sign up?

  • When we have an estimator go out to provide an estimate the goal is to have the homeowner sign up that day. If

the estimator has failed to sell the lead at the appointment the lead will then become what is called a rehash.

  • If an estimator sells the homeowner at the time of the initial appointment but he/she changes their mind and

cancels the job this will now become a rehash job

  • If multiple appointment setters have made contact for rehash

o The bonus will be split evenly between the appointment setters o Over 1 month of no contact, it becomes a new rehash & the latest appointment setter will receive full compensation.

  • Scripting must be followed & all questions need to be asked
  • Anything under 75% of retail - cannot set

What DOES NOT Qualify a rehash sign up?

  • Follow up sales appointments by sales managers
  • New appointments set that the sales manager has been in contact with
  • Customer calls in to move forward with the project
  • Customer only wants estimate emailed over because they didn’t receive it
  • If customer is already wanting to move forward with project

What is the responsibility of the appointment setter with rehash leads?

  • Rehash prospects will automatically filter into the queue. It is the appointment setters job to verify that the

appointment or canceled job date is from the prior day.

  • The appointments setters will call the rehash queue to try and touch base with the customer to see if they are

still interested in having Friendly Fence & Roofing to perform the work they inquired about, using the provided scripting.

What happens when a rehash customer wants to sign up with us?

  • If the customer says “i would like to move forward with the estimate i was given” or anything related to

wanting Friendly Fence & Roofing to take on the project the appointment setter will send the homeowners information to the sales manager.

KPI Scorecard Playbook This outlines the core KPI Scorecard elements within our Standard Operating Procedures. It encompasses universal rules, CSR, Rehash/ISR, Sales, and Leadership KPIs, along with Sales Activity Standards and basic business principles.

Key Areas:

  • Universal Rules: Foundational guidelines for all team members.
  • CSR KPI Scorecard: Metrics for Customer Service Representatives.
  • Rehash KPI Scorecard: Metrics for Inside Sales Representatives.
  • Sales KPI Scorecard: Metrics for the Sales Team.
  • Leadership Review KPIs: Metrics reviewed by Leadership.
  • Sales Activity Standards: Expected sales activities and benchmarks.
  • Core business values and operational principles.

Purpose of This Playbook This document establishes clear non-negotiable performance standards across Sales, Marketing, Operations, Inventory and Leadership.

KPIs are minimum expectations not goals. Accountability removes ambiguity. Consistency drives predictable results.

How To Use This Document

  • KPIs are reviewed weekly or monthly as defined
  • Missed KPIs trigger coaching not debate
  • Barriers are logged in the Gap Log
  • Leaders own enforcement and consistency
  • Standards apply to everyone without exception

If it is not measured it cannot be coached. If it is not enforced it is not a standard.

Universal Accountability Rules

  • Minimum standards not stretch goals
  • Training ramps are defined and finite
  • Data drives conversations not emotion
  • Leaders own misses first
  • Support is documented through the Gap Log

Strong standards raise performance and filter talent naturally.

CSR KPI SCORECARD

Role Objective: Create consistent opportunity flow through disciplined call activity.

Minimum Performance Standards

                  KPI                               Standard             Review
 Inbound and outbound calls                244 calls per day         Daily
 Booking Rate                              90%+ - Inbound            Daily

30%+ - Outbound

 Booking accuracy                          Zero preventable errors   Weekly
 Lead disposition                          100% completed            Daily

Non Negotiable Standard Call volume is the job. Coaching begins only after 244 calls per day is met.

CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE KPIs Revenue protection and referrals

KPI Healthy Standard

Net promoter score 60+

Online review velocity Consistent monthly

Review response rate 100% w/in 24 hours

Complaint resolution time <24 hours

Warranty claim rate Tracked

Rehash/ISR KPI SCORECARD

Role Objective: Recover revenue from unsold opportunities reduce lead waste and maximize marketing ROI.

Core Definitions

ISR: Inbound Sales Representative responsible for outbound follow up on unsold estimates, unbooked calls and aged leads.

Rehash Program: Structured process to re-engage no sales cancelled calls and estimates that did not close the same day.

Minimum Performance Standards

                   KPI                        Standard            Review Cadence
Saved calls rate                        15-25%                Weekly
Rebook rate from no sale follow up      10-20%                Weekly
Revenue recovered per ISR               Tracked weekly        Weekly
Average days to save                    <7 days               Weekly

If the saved call rate is 10% the script timing or ownership is broken.

Outbound Activity KPIs

                   KPI                            Standard          Review Cadence
Outbound calls per ISR per day            75-125                   Daily
Contacts made per day                     15-30                    Daily
Contact rate                                 20-30%                  Weekly
Voicemail drop usage                         100%                    Daily

Speed and volume matter more than perfection.

Follow Up Discipline KPIs

               KPI                     Standard             Review Cadence
No sale follow up attempted       100%                  Daily
Follow up attempts per lead       6-8 attempts          Weekly
First follow up timing            Within 24 hours       Daily
Multi channel follow up           Call/text/email       Weekly

If it is not attempted, it was abandoned.

Revenue KPIs

               KPI                           Standard            Review Cadence
Revenue per saved call            Tracked                       Weekly
Cost per recovered dollar         Lower than Paid CPA           Monthly
Rehash close rate                 10-20%                        Monthly
ISR influenced revenue            Tracked                       Monthly

ISR revenue should always outperform cold marketing ROI.

Pipeline Management KPIs

KPI Standard

Open rehash leads aged <30 days 100%

Aged leads <30 days Reviewed weekly

Lost leads with no follow up Zero

Unworked leads are silent profit leaks.

Quality and Compliance KPIs

KPI Standard

Script adherence Monitored weekly

CRM notes completed 100%

Call recordings reviewed 3x/week

Sales handoff documentation 100%

Rehash without documentation creates chaos downstream.

If a KPI does not affect

  • Profit
  • Cash
  • Capacity
  • Customer trust
  • Exit value

It is not a KPI.

Sales Manager – Job Description We are seeking a driven Sales Leader to build, manage, and scale a high performing sales team. This role is responsible for creating a repeatable sales process, coaching sales professionals, and driving predictable revenue growth.

This is a full time position. Typical work hours are Monday through Friday, with flexibility required based on sales activity.

Key Responsibilities

Sales Leadership: Lead, coach, and manage the sales team to hit revenue targets. Conduct regular training, role play, and performance reviews. Recruit, onboard, and develop top sales talent.

Sales Process and Performance: Build and enforce a structured sales process. Train on scripts, objection handling, and closing strategies. Track conversion rates, close rates, and pipeline performance. Forecast sales performance and report results to leadership.

Cross Functional Collaboration: Work closely with marketing and operations to ensure alignment. Provide feedback on lead quality and customer insights.

Qualifications

  • Bachelor’s degree preferred.
  • 5+ years of sales experience with at least 2 years in leadership.
  • Proven track record of building and leading sales teams.
  • Strong communication and coaching skills.
  • Experience in home services, construction, or roofing preferred.

What We Offer

  • Competitive base salary plus performance incentives.
  • Growth opportunities within a scaling organization.
  • A performance driven culture focused on results.

How to Apply

Interested candidates should submit a resume and a brief cover letter highlighting relevant experience and interest in the role.

Dear [EMPLOYEE NAME]:

We are pleased to extend you an offer of at-will employment, upon the terms set forth in this employment offer letter. You will be employed by Friendly Fence & Roofing SC in the full-time position of Sales Leader, reporting to Mike Shelly, with an anticipated commencement date of 3/3/2025 or mutually agreed upon date. You will be based out of the GA location. You will be required to carry out your duties faithfully, honestly, diligently, and to the best of your abilities. You will be required to devote your full time and efforts to the Company. Your responsibilities will be as directed by the Company.

Rate of Pay-You will earn an Annual Salary of $100,000. You will earn .033% on all monthly Friendly Fence & Roofing SC completed Installed Revenue. This is to be paid on the first pay period after the 15th of each month. 2.5% of net sales of the Company when Friendly Fence & Roofing sells. You must be actively employed at the time of sale to receive percentage payout. If you resign or are terminated you will not be entitled to any earnings. 8% commission on sales sold by you of the total completed and collected revenue on the jobs sold. If gross profit margin falls beneath 40% no commissions will be paid. Gross is calculated by the following: Gross Profit Margin = (Revenue – Cost of Goods Sold) / Revenue x 100. Gross Profit Margin is calculated after Sales commission, Materials, Sub pay, Finance fees and trash disposal are calculated. 4% of all ride along sales, of the total completed and collected revenue on the jobs sold. If gross profit margin falls beneath 40% no commissions will be paid.

Compensation is paid weekly and direct deposit is required. Our pay period does follow a “week behind” schedule. Your first paycheck will be received on 3/14/2025.

Paid Time Off (PTO): After the expiration of your 90-day Introductory Period, you will be eligible to utilize any earned PTO, which accrues at 6.7 hours of PTO per month employed during your tenure of service. Your PTO allotment will be capped at 80 hours.

Benefits: This full-time position offers a full complement of benefits plans including Medical, Dental, and Vision insurance wherein the Company covers $375 towards the total monthly medical Expenses. We also offer a 401k program with up to a 4% match. These benefits will become effective following the completion of your 90-day Introductory Period.

Immigration Compliance Requirements: For compliance with Federal immigration law, you will be required to provide to the Company documentary evidence of your identity and eligibility for you to work in the United States. Such documentation must be provided to the Company within three (3) business days of your date of hire, or your employment with the Company may be terminated.

As a material term of your offer of employment, you will be required to sign and adhere to the Company’s standard Confidentiality and Non-Solicitation Agreement (“Agreement”).

Your employment with the Company is for an indefinite period of time and you are an employee-at-will. This means that you have the right to terminate your employment at any time for any (or no) reason, with or without notice, and the Company retains the same right. Any promise of employment for a definite period of time, or any promise that modifies your status as an employee-at-will, must be in writing and approved by the CEO of the Company. Unless otherwise agreed in writing, and signed by the Company CEO, these provisions for termination of your employment shall continue to apply even if your position, salary, benefits, or other terms of your employment are changed.

INTRODUCTION

Hello! We are excited to welcome you to Friendly Fence & Roofing.

Here at Friendly Fence & Roofing, we pride ourselves on creating a warm, team-focused atmosphere where cooperation and support are central to our operations. We hope that you will find our company to be a welcoming, engaging, and fair place to work!

This handbook presents a number of key concepts for our company. Some of these represent legal standards that we adhere to. Other aspects outline our expectations for employees and what employees can expect from us. We strongly encourage you to read this handbook in its entirety and keep it in a location where you can easily access it as a valuable resource and reference.

SECTION 1: ADMINISTRATIVE POLICIES AND PROCEDURES

Employment At-Will
